analysis.one_liner: Creates a government health insurance program covering everyone living in the United States, replacing private health insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 38 cosponsors but was never given a hearing or vote; it died in a House subcommittee when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put every person living in the U.S. into a single government-run health insurance program covering doctor visits, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, and long-term care, with no deductibles, copayments, or premiums. Private insurers would be barred from selling coverage that duplicates it. Funding would come from existing federal health spending plus new taxes: higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a modest payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond trades.
analysis.who_benefits: All U.S. residents, insured and uninsured alike. Everyone would get comprehensive coverage with no out-of-pocket costs at the doctor or pharmacy, free choice of any participating doctor or hospital, and no denial for pre-existing conditions. The uninsured would gain coverage entirely; the insured would trade premiums, deductibles, and network restrictions for taxes, likely paying less overall. Hospital billing departments and displaced insurance clerical workers were promised first priority in retraining and job placement in the new system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident needing health care

how_it_helps.text: All individuals residing in the United States would be covered, receiving a national health insurance card and a comprehensive standard of care.

Coverage includes primary care, inpatient and outpatient care, emergency care, prescription drugs, long-term care, mental health, dental, vision, and substance abuse treatment, with no deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing.
Patients would have free choice of participating doctors, clinics, and hospitals anywhere in the country.
The program would negotiate prescription drug prices annually, run a formulary favoring generics, and allow clinicians and patients to petition to add or remove drugs.

Funding would draw on higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a modest payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions, alongside savings from reduced paperwork and bulk drug procurement.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers. The bill replaces premiums and out-of-pocket costs with taxes: an income tax increase on the top 5% of earners, a modest payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond trades, plus existing federal health dollars redirected from Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP. For-profit hospitals and clinics that chose to participate would have to convert to nonprofit status, with owners compensated only for real property and equipment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, especially the top 5% of earners

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no dollar figures for its funding: it authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' and lists tax sources without estimating whether they would fully cover the program's cost, so its affordability was never tested.

Private health insurers would be barred from selling coverage duplicating the program's benefits, effectively ending most of the private health insurance industry, a massive economic transition even though displaced clerical workers were promised first priority in retraining and placement.

It declared an effective date of January 1, 2005, less than two years after introduction, an unusually short runway for converting the entire U.S. health system, including a 15-year phased conversion of investor-owned providers.

Hospitals would move to annually negotiated global budgets and clinicians to a negotiated fee schedule or salary, replacing market payment with government-set budgets, which critics argued could constrain provider supply and investment in new facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's promise was large and simple: everyone covered, nothing owed at the point of care, and private insurers removed from the middle. The honest counterweight is that it never produced a funding plan with real numbers, so the trade of private premiums for taxes was unverified, and the transition would have been one of the largest economic reorganizations in U.S. history. As a policy blueprint it was thorough; as legislation it was an opening statement rather than a workable bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2003, referred to four House committees, sent to the Health Subcommittee a month later, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers of Michigan introduced the United States National Health Insurance Act on February 11, 2003, joined by 25 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Resources, and Veterans' Affairs — which is itself a hurdle, since any committee can hold a bill.
In March 2003 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
The bill ended with 38 cosponsors, 37 Democrats and 1 Independent, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, pharmaceutical manufacturers, and for-profit hospital operators kept the existing system intact. Americans continued paying premiums, deductibles, and copayments, and the roughly 40 million uninsured at the time remained without coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, drug makers, for-profit providers

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in June 2003.

for.name: 37 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 38 total cosponsors including one Independent.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Resources, and Veterans' Affairs Committees (Republican majority)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; after its referral to the Health Subcommittee in March 2003, no further action occurred for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling House committees and the floor calendar, 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to sit in committee without action through the end of the Congress; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Democrats (37) or an Independent (1); no Republican backed it, and the Republican majority that controlled the bill's four committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for private insurers to sell coverage duplicating the program's benefits, which would end their core business of covering basic medical care. Insurers profit by collecting premiums and limiting payments for care, so their interest in blocking a program that eliminates both ran directly against the public's interest in cheaper, universal coverage.

The program would negotiate drug prices annually, promote generics, and steer prescribing through a formulary, replacing the industry's ability to set prices market by market. Drug prices are a leading driver of what ordinary people pay for care.

Investor-owned providers could participate only by converting to nonprofit status over 15 years, with owners compensated only for real property and equipment, not lost profits. Nonprofit hospitals would keep operating but under government global budgets instead of negotiated charges to patients and insurers.

industries.industry: Health insurance administrative and billing workforce
industries.note: The bill would eliminate hundreds of thousands of billing and claims jobs as paperwork collapsed, but it explicitly promised displaced clerical and administrative workers first priority in retraining and job placement in the new system.
